body.title: Personal statement
body.prompt: Describe your background and why you chose this programme (max. 600 words).
body.body:
I grew up above my mother's tailoring shop, where every evening ended with the ledger open on the cutting table. She taught me that a business is a promise kept in small numbers, and I have been keeping books for her since I was fourteen.

In my final year of school I rebuilt that ledger as a spreadsheet that three neighbouring shops now use. The work showed me how much I do not know: pricing, credit, how a shop becomes a company. That is why I am applying to study in Busan, a port city whose trade I have followed through the fabric my mother buys.

I have studied Korean for two years and passed the level this programme asks for. I expect the first semester to be difficult, and I have planned for it: I will take the university's academic Korean course alongside my major and join a study group from the first week.

After graduating I intend to return home and turn the family shop into a registered supplier for regional retailers. I would be the first person in my family to earn a university degree, and I intend to use it where it will be seen.

body.title: Study plan
body.prompt: Outline your plan of study by semester.
body.body:
Semester 1–2: complete the foundation courses and the academic Korean track, aiming for TOPIK 5 by the end of the first year.

Semester 3–4: choose the concentration, take accounting and statistics in Korean, and apply for a part-time research assistant position in the department.

Semester 5–6: a one-semester exchange or an internship arranged through the career centre; begin the graduation project proposal.

Semester 7–8: complete the graduation project on small-retailer supply chains between Korea and Southeast Asia, and sit the final language certification.

body.title: Personal statement
body.prompt: Describe your background and why you chose this programme (max. 600 words).
body.body:
I grew up above my mother's tailoring shop, where every evening ended with the ledger open on the cutting table. She taught me that a business is a promise kept in small numbers, and I have been keeping books for her since I was fourteen.

In my final year of school I rebuilt that ledger as a spreadsheet that three neighbouring shops now use. The work showed me how much I do not know: pricing, credit, how a shop becomes a company. That is why I am applying to study in Busan, a port city whose trade I have followed through the fabric my mother buys.

I have studied Korean for two years and passed the level this programme asks for. I expect the first semester to be difficult, and I have planned for it: I will take the university's academic Korean course alongside my major and join a study group from the first week.

After graduating I intend to return home and turn the family shop into a registered supplier for regional retailers. I would be the first person in my family to earn a university degree, and I intend to use it where it will be seen.

body.title: Study plan
body.prompt: Outline your plan of study by semester.
body.body:
Semester 1–2: complete the foundation courses and the academic Korean track, aiming for TOPIK 5 by the end of the first year.

Semester 3–4: choose the concentration, take accounting and statistics in Korean, and apply for a part-time research assistant position in the department.

Semester 5–6: a one-semester exchange or an internship arranged through the career centre; begin the graduation project proposal.

Semester 7–8: complete the graduation project on small-retailer supply chains between Korea and Southeast Asia, and sit the final language certification.
